title: The race for leadership talent in India’s hospital and IVF sector

thbAction: Map the news to THB's provider CRM for referral growth, patient lifecycle engagement, and multi-facility relationship management across hospital and provider networks.
contentHtml:
India’s healthcare sector is witnessing significant investment activity. According to the EY-IVCA monthly PE/VC roundup, healthcare investments grew 621 per cent YoY during July–September 2026, with 28 deals valued at US$3.1 billion, making it the second-largest sector for investment after infrastructure.

A significant share of this capital is being directed towards hospital networks and organised fertility chains, both characterised by fragmented ownership, unmet demand and considerable consolidation opportunities. Investors are acquiring established platforms to expand their networks, integrate regional businesses and professionalise founder-led operations. However, delivering on these ambitions will depend increasingly on experienced leadership talent capable of managing scale and driving sustainable growth.

Where the investment is going

Recent transactions show where investors are placing their bets. Hospitals accounted for US$1.8 billion of healthcare investments during the quarter. The largest transaction was KKR’s US$1.4 billion acquisition of Medicover India, with a network of 26+ hospitals and over 6000 beds across India, that takes KKR’s bed count in southern India close to 10,000.

India’s IVF market is estimated at US$1 billion, growing at 13–16 per cent annually. The country performs approximately 210 IVF cycles per million people, compared with more than 2,000 in Europe. Nearly 90 per cent of its 6,500 fertility clinics operate independently, presenting significant consolidation opportunities.

Why leadership is central to value creation

At current valuations, market growth alone will not deliver the returns investors expect. Investors are underwriting these deals on operating improvement, and every lever in that plan comes with a leadership requirement attached: bolt-on acquisitions, better revenue per bed, a centralised finance and procurement function, and new speciality programmes. Each needs an executive who can turn an investment thesis into operational and financial results.

Many hospitals and fertility centres have evolved as founder-led enterprises, built around the reputation and clinical expertise of individual doctors. While successful as regional businesses, managing networks of 20 or 30 facilities across different cities and regulatory environments requires a more institutionalised approach. Expanding organisations need leaders who can standardise processes, establish accountability and maintain consistency in patient care without compromising clinical quality and relationships.

The fertility sector illustrates this well. One of India’s largest IVF and fertility chains reported broadly flat cycle volumes last year despite its extensive network. Adding centres does not necessarily translate into patient growth. Clinical outcomes, patient trust and referral networks remain fundamental to performance, making leadership at both corporate and centre levels critical.

The evolving leadership mandate

As healthcare platforms grow, expectations from senior executives are changing. The traditional separation between clinical leadership and business management is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.

India has 1.3 hospital beds per 1,000 people, against a global median of 2.9. Leading private hospital chains plan to add more than 38,000 beds by 2030. For hospital networks, the COO’s mandate extends beyond individual facilities to managing geographically distributed operations, improving capacity utilisation, patient experience and consistency across hospitals.

The CFO’s role is becoming more strategic, encompassing acquisition economics, integration, financial governance and preparation for an eventual listing or sponsor exit. In February 2026, Gaudium IVF became India’s first listed fertility company, with its IPO subscribed more than seven times. This demonstrates the growing relevance of public market readiness.

The CHRO is assuming a more central role. The availability of high-quality doctors, nurses and specialised professionals directly influences an organisation’s capacity to expand and generate revenue. Building talent pipelines, succession plans and performance frameworks is therefore a business priority.

In fertility services, competition for experienced specialists, embryologists and centre heads is particularly intense. Their expertise, clinical outcomes and relationships with patients and referring doctors directly influence centre performance. When a consolidator acquires a respected regional clinic, the founder-doctor’s reputation is often an important part of the value being acquired. Retaining that clinician through and beyond the transaction can materially influence its success.

Integration, succession and broadening the talent pool

With consolidation accelerating, integration capability is becoming an important leadership differentiator.

Nova IVF has expanded into Kerala through Craft Fertility, Indira IVF has acquired Banker IVF in Gujarat, and KKR-backed Baby Memorial Hospital has acquired Hyderabad’s Star Hospitals. These transactions require leaders who can align organisational cultures, harmonise clinical and administrative processes, retain critical talent and establish common operating standards. Executives with proven multi-site integration experience remain relatively scarce within Indian healthcare.

Succession planning is equally important. Founder-led businesses often depend on a handful of senior executives or clinicians. Building a strong second line of leadership is essential for continuity and reducing individual dependencies as organisations expand.

This also presents an opportunity to broaden the talent search universe. While clinical leadership must remain rooted in healthcare, business and functional leaders from consumer, hospitality, retail and other multi-location service industries bring relevant experience in network expansion, customer experience, operational standardisation and workforce management. Such executives can contribute across operations, finance, HR and business transformation, provided they adapt to an environment where clinical judgement, patient safety and ethical standards remain paramount.

Talent will determine long-term success

Growing investment in hospitals and fertility services presents an opportunity to strengthen India’s healthcare infrastructure and expand access to organised care. However, growth will require as much attention to leadership capability as to capital deployment.

From an executive search perspective, demand is increasing for leaders who combine commercial orientation, operational depth, experience of managing scale and the ability to institutionalise businesses without compromising their clinical foundations. For investors and healthcare organisations, leadership planning must become integral to investment and growth strategies, rather than an exercise undertaken after an acquisition.

Ultimately, organisations that build strong management teams, develop leadership pipelines and deliver consistent patient experiences will be better positioned to realise the full value of their investments. In a sector where trust, clinical quality and operational consistency are fundamental, attracting and retaining the right leadership talent will be as critical to long-term value creation as acquiring and expanding assets.
